newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--Heat stocks seen nearing surplus in APIs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--Heat stocks seen nearing surplus in APIs.

text.p: An expected rise in distillate stocks in Tuesday's oil inventory report from the American Petroleum Institute (API) may signal a surplus in distillate inventories by month's end, traders said.

"If we don't get a prolonged cold spell the way we did last year, the distillate deficit may be gone by the end of January," said Cargill Investor Services analyst Thomas Blakeslee. An average of trader estimates calls for distillate stocks (comprised of heating oil and diesel) to grow by 1.5 million barrels for the January 3 week being reported.

"I expect there to have been a drop in demand while supplies remain constant," Blakeslee said, noting distillate output should outstrip demand which was seen off due to unseasonably warm temperatures in many U.S. regions last week.

Estimates for distillate stocks ranged from off 900,000 barrels to up three million barrels. A drop in demand was also supposed to boost gasoline stocks by 1.7 million barrels, with trader estimates ranging from up one million to 2.8 million barrels.
Crude stocks were expected to decline by less than one million barrels as imports eased.
"Crude imports should back off a bit and after last week's solid build, we could see a bit of a correction," said ING Derivatives analyst Tom Bentz.
Estimates for crude were wide as usual, ranging from a draw of two million barrels to a build of 1.5 million barrels.
Crude stocks and distillate stocks have wiped out a good portion of their year-over-year deficit, with distillate stocks building amid record output and tepid demand for over the past month.
Crude stocks are now 7.75 million barrels below year ago after being off 21.9 million barrels in late December.
Distillate stocks are now 5.40 million barrels below the year ago level after being off 19.8 million barrels in early August.

A harsh winter in 1995 left distillate stocks historically low. Refiners kept stocks lean due to a "just-in-time" inventory strategy which seeks to cut storage costs through low stocks. Fears of a heat shortage this winter helped send heating oil prices to post-Gulf War highs by October.
"A build in distillate stocks tonight would be minorly bearish, but a surplus would be a much bigger deal," said Blakeslee.
Blakeslee said a surplus could occur if the past month's temperature pattern of short cold snaps amid moderate weather persisted this winter.
If refiners exited the winter with a distillate stock surplus, it would help ensure ample supply for next year, depressing heating oil prices in the long term, dealers said.
